notes.meaning: Jesus told His followers that this was His final time drinking wine before His death. The next time He would drink it would be new in the kingdom of God, pointing forward to heavenly joy. The Lord's Supper looks back to His death and ahead to this great future banquet.

After the meal was finished, Jesus and the disciples sang a hymn of praise together and walked out to the Mount of Olives. Singing praises right before His arrest shows His calm trust in the Father's plan. He did not hide, but willingly went out to meet His suffering.

Jesus warned the disciples that every one of them would abandon Him that night, fulfilling the Old Testament prophecy that the shepherd would be struck and the sheep scattered. Even so, He gave them immediate comfort by promising that He would rise again. After His resurrection, He promised to go ahead of them to gather them back together in Galilee.

Peter spoke up and insisted that he would never fall away, even if all the other disciples did. He felt sure that his own courage was strong enough to face any danger. His boast showed that he trusted his own willpower rather than depending on God's strength.

Jesus told Peter plainly that his fall would happen that very night, before the rooster crowed twice. Instead of standing firm, Peter would deny knowing Jesus three separate times. Jesus knew Peter's hidden weakness far better than Peter knew himself.

Instead of listening to the warning, Peter argued even more strongly that he would die with Jesus rather than disown Him. The rest of the disciples made the exact same promise. They were sincere in what they said, but they did not yet realize how quickly human strength fails in the face of fear.

They arrived at a garden named Gethsemane, a word that means an olive oil press. Jesus told most of the disciples to sit and wait while He went a short distance away to pray. He chose this quiet, familiar spot not to hide from His enemies, but to prepare for His suffering by seeking His Father.

Jesus brought Peter, James, and John deeper into the garden with Him. Suddenly, He was seized with great horror, shock, and deep distress. This intense grief showed the real struggle of His human soul as He faced the full weight of the cross.

Jesus told the three friends that His soul was crushed with sorrow, even to the point of death. He asked them to remain there and keep watch with Him. Even though He was the Lord, He welcomed the presence and comfort of His close companions in His darkest hour.

Moving a little further away, Jesus threw Himself to the ground to pray. He asked that, if it were possible, this terrible hour of suffering might pass Him by. His posture showed total lowliness before God as He faced the dreadful cost of human salvation.

Jesus addressed God with deep love as "Abba, Father," acknowledging that God has the power to do all things. He pleaded for this cup of bitter suffering and divine wrath to be taken away, yet He chose to obey the Father's will above His own. This prayer reveals His complete surrender to God's rescue plan for sinners.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Christ has two distinct wills, one divine and one human, and that in Gethsemane His human will felt the natural fear of death but freely submitted to the divine will.

notes.meaning: When Jesus returned to the three disciples, He found them asleep instead of praying. He spoke directly to Peter by his old name, Simon, asking if he could not stay awake for even a single hour. The very man who had claimed he would die for Jesus could not even stay alert to support Him.

Jesus urged them to stay alert and pray so that they would not fall into temptation. He explained that while their inner spirit was willing to do right, their physical bodies and human nature were weak. Good intentions are never enough to overcome trials without God's help through prayer.

Jesus went away again and prayed using the exact same words of plea and surrender. Repeating His request showed His persistent, earnest faith rather than any doubt. He gives believers an example to keep bringing our deepest burdens to God over and over.

When Jesus came back a second time, the disciples were fast asleep again because their eyes were heavy with fatigue. They were so embarrassed by their failure that they had nothing to say for themselves. Their human weakness kept them from standing with their Master in His hour of need.

Jesus returned the third time and told them that the time for watching was now past. The decisive moment had arrived, and the Son of Man was being handed over to sinful men. There was no more time for resting because the enemy had reached the garden.

Jesus told the disciples to stand up so they could go out to meet the approaching danger. Instead of running away to protect Himself, He stepped boldly toward His enemies. His actions showed that He was not an unwilling victim, but remained in calm control of what was happening.

Before Jesus had even finished speaking, Judas showed up with a large mob carrying swords and clubs. This crowd had been sent by the chief priests, teachers of the law, and elders of Israel. Judas had lived and traveled with Jesus as one of the twelve apostles, yet he chose to lead the enemies who wanted to kill Him.

Judas had arranged a secret signal with the crowd beforehand so they would not grab the wrong person in the dark. He told them to arrest the man he kissed and to take Him away under close guard. He turned a customary sign of love and respect into a tool for betrayal.

Judas went straight up to Jesus, greeted Him warmly as his Teacher, and kissed Him. He put on an outward show of affection while delivering Jesus into the hands of an armed mob. This hypocritical greeting exposed the true darkness of Judas's actions.

The armed men moved in, grabbed Jesus with rough hands, and took Him into custody. The religious leaders had wanted to do this for a long time, and now their plot seemed to succeed. Jesus allowed them to arrest Him because He was freely giving His life according to God's will.

One of the disciples standing near Jesus pulled out a sword, struck the high priest's servant, and sliced off his ear. Peter acted with rash bravery to defend his Lord, likely aiming to hit the man's head. Yet physical violence and worldly weapons are not the way Christ's kingdom fights.

Jesus asked the crowd why they came out with swords and clubs to capture Him as if He were a dangerous criminal. He had never used violence, and coming armed was completely unnecessary. Their armed raid under the cover of night only showed their own cowardice and guilty conscience.
